title: Count how many times a given number appears in an array (loop + counter).
shortTitle: Count how many times a given number appears in an array

s1_definition.profdef: Counting occurrences is a linear scan where you walk the array and increment a counter each time an element equals the target value. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space. The only subtlety for money is comparing with `compareTo` (value equality) rather than `equals` (which also checks scale).
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh wants to know how many times exactly Rs.5000 was debited from his account SAV2001 this month, perhaps a recurring subscription. He reads each transaction in his passbook, and every time the amount is exactly Rs.5000 he makes a tally mark. At the end, the number of tally marks is the count.
s1_definition.oneliner: Walk the array once with a counter, and add one to the counter every time an element matches the target.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Counting occurrences is a linear scan where you walk the array and increment a counter each time an element equals the target value. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space. The only subtlety for money is comparing with `compareTo` (value equality) rather than `equals` (which also checks scale).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh wants to know how many times exactly Rs.5000 was debited from his account SAV2001 this month, perhaps a recurring subscription. He reads each transaction in his passbook, and every time the amount is exactly Rs.5000 he makes a tally mark. At the end, the number of tally marks is the count.

**One line to remember:** Walk the array once with a counter, and add one to the counter every time an element matches the target.

sections.s2_technical:
You start a counter at zero. You loop through every element and compare it with the target. If they match, you increment the counter. There is no early exit, because the same value can appear multiple times anywhere in the array, so you must check every element.

For money, comparison must use `compareTo` returning zero, not `equals`. The reason is that `new BigDecimal("5000")` and `new BigDecimal("5000.00")` are the same amount but are NOT equal under `equals` because their scale differs. Using `target.compareTo(current) == 0` treats both as the same amount, which is what a bank customer expects. For plain `int` arrays you would simply use `==`.

Time complexity is O(n) because you examine every element. Space is O(1) because you keep only the counter. A senior nuance is deciding what "equal" means for your domain — for currency it is value equality, so `compareTo` is the correct tool.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India offers Rajesh a feature: "How many times was exactly Rs.5000 debited this month?" so he can spot recurring charges. The system holds his transaction amounts and must count how many equal the target. This is exactly how the count-occurrences algorithm works — loop and tally matches.

Problem 2 — The amounts might be stored with different scales, such as `5000` and `5000.00`, but the customer means the same amount. This is exactly why we compare with compareTo and value equality, not with equals, so scale differences do not cause us to miss a match.

The code has an `Account` holding amounts and a `TransactionCounter` class with a `countOccurrences` method. The demo counts how many times Rs.5000 appears.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: amounts `[5000.00, 1200.00, 5000, 300.00, 5000.00]`, target `5000`.

Step 1 — Counter starts at 0.

Step 2 — Element `5000.00` compared to `5000` by value: equal. Counter becomes 1.

Step 3 — Element `1200.00` not equal. Counter stays 1.

Step 4 — Element `5000` equal (same scale). Counter becomes 2.

Step 5 — Element `300.00` not equal. Counter stays 2.

Step 6 — Element `5000.00` equal. Counter becomes 3.

Step 7 — Loop ends. Return 3. Note the scale difference between `5000` and `5000.00` did not cause a miss because we used compareTo.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Rs.5000 debited 3 times for Rajesh Kumar (SAV2001)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Counting how many times a value appears in an array is a straightforward linear scan with a counter. I start a counter at zero, loop through every element, and increment the counter each time the element matches the target. There is no early exit because the target can appear anywhere, even multiple times, so I must inspect every element. The time complexity is linear and the space complexity is constant.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this to build a recurring charge detector. Rajesh wanted to know how many times exactly five thousand rupees was debited this month so he could spot a subscription he forgot about. I loop through his transaction amounts and tally each one that equals five thousand.

The important nuance here is how I compare money. I compare BigDecimal values using the compareTo method and check for a result of zero, rather than using the equals method. The reason is that five thousand written as plain five thousand and five thousand written with two decimal places are the same amount of money, but the equals method considers them different because their scale differs. By using compareTo I treat them as equal in value, which is exactly what the customer means, so a scale difference in how the amount was stored never causes me to miss a genuine match.
